blocks.text: There are two types of solids on the basis of the way their particles are arranged: crystalline solids and amorphous solids.

blocks.caption: Comparison of crystalline and amorphous solids (Table 5.5)
rows: Melt sharply at their melting points
No sharp melting point; melt over a range of temperature
Anisotropic: properties depend on the direction of measurement
Isotropic: properties do not depend on direction

blocks.alt: Three boxes of particles: a neat purple grid for a crystalline solid, a jumble of orange dots with one small ordered patch marked crystallite for an amorphous solid, and green rods lying roughly parallel for a liquid crystal, each with notes. Below, a chain solid to liquid to gas with the molar heats of fusion and vaporization on the arrows.
blocks.caption: Crystalline solids, amorphous solids and liquid crystals, with the energetics of phase changes (original diagram after Table 5.5 and topics 5.10 and 5.13).
blocks.long_description: A crystalline solid repeats its arrangement over long distances, giving definite shapes, sharp melting points, cleavage planes and direction-dependent properties. An amorphous solid has only small ordered regions, so it melts over a range, has no definite heat of fusion, can be moulded and is the same in every direction. A liquid crystal has rod-like molecules that stay roughly parallel while flowing, so it combines the flow and viscosity of a liquid with the optical properties and anisotropy of a crystal. Melting and vaporizing absorb the molar heats of fusion and vaporization.

blocks.prompt: Glass is sometimes called a supercooled liquid rather than a true solid. Which rows of the table support that description?
blocks.explanation: Glass is amorphous: it has no long-range order, no sharp melting point (it softens over a range of temperature) and is isotropic, like a liquid whose molecules have simply stopped moving. A true crystalline solid would show long-range order, a sharp melting point and anisotropy.

items: Two types by arrangement: crystalline (definite shape, sharp melting point, anisotropic, long-range order) and amorphous (lumps or powder, melts over a range, isotropic, no long-range order).
